newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity rises on weather, NW line talk.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity rises on weather, NW line talk.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were higher Monday on expected cooling demand in the Southwest and talk of a possible reduction in capacity on the Pacific Intertie transmission system, industry sources said.
"A lot of it is the weather, and people are watching the Pacific Intertie situation," a New York futures trader said.

As of 1305 EDT, July Palo Verde (PV) was up $1.47 per megawatt hour (MWh) at $29.15, traded $28.50-29.25, while August was up $1.14 at a session high of $31.00 after slipping as low as $30.50 per MWh.
July California Oregon Border (COB) was up $1.20 at $19.00 following exchanges of $18.35-19.25, while August was up 89 cents at a day's high of $21.80 after trading as low as $21.50 per MWh.
NYMEX said that as of 1215 EDT an estimated total of 278 COB and 217 PV contracts traded.

Temperatures in the Pacific Northwest were expected to be one to five degrees below normal early in the week, then were forecast to be near normal for the middle of the week and cool again to just below normal late in the week. Clouds and showers were expected early in the week.
Normal summer weather was expected in the Southwest through the week.
Coastal cities from Seattle to San Diego would see temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit area, while inland centers like Phoenix and Tuscon would be covered by triple-digit heat by mid-week.

Some upward pressure on futures was seen from expecations a Western Systems Coordinating Council committee this week would propose a summertime rating for the Pacific Intertie at 6,900 megawatt (MW), 300 MW below from current level to insure electricity reliability.
In the meantime, Bonneville Power Administration suggested summer transmission capacity on the intertie be reduced to 6,300 MW from the current limit of 7,200 MW.
As of 1300, NYMEX July Henry Hub natural gas futures were trading up 2.1 cents at $2.17 per million British thermal units.
Seperately, about 3,000 MW of coal-fired capacity was planned to restart over the week after unplanned repair shutdowns and planned maintenance outages.
A 750 MW unit 1 at the Mohave coal-fired power plant in Nevada was seen back on line Tuesday after being shut over the weekend for maintenance work.
The 540 MW unit 4 at the San Juan coal-fired unit in New Mexico was restarted Saturday after being taken off line June 6 for maintenance.
Also, an 875 MW unit 1 at the Intermountain coal-fired power plant in Delta, Utah was restarted Sunday after being taken off line Friday to repair a tube leak.
The 750 MW unit 5 at the Four Corners coal fired plant in New Mexico was restarted Monday after being shut Thursday for maintenance.
Moreover, the 1,112 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state was expected to resume power production next week, ahead of an original schedule.
